opus-5.5.text:
I think it's broadly right, but the reasoning matters more than the slogan.

If AGI means a system that can operate in the real world the way people do, it can't live only in text. Humans learn a huge amount from vision, sound, and physical interaction before we ever learn to read. Text is a highly compressed, abstract record of human knowledge. That's why language models got so far so fast. But it's also lossy. Many things about space, motion, cause and effect, and how objects behave are never fully written down, because to humans they're too obvious to mention.

So yes, I believe a truly general intelligence needs to perceive the world directly, not just through descriptions of it.

That said, I'd push back on one common assumption: that you just add more modalities and intelligence emerges. So far, the core reasoning ability, the "thinking" part, has mostly come from language. Language is where abstraction, planning, and logic are densest. Many current multimodal systems are really a language model with perception attached. They can describe an image, but they don't think visually in a deep way.

The harder and more interesting question is whether multimodal data can actually improve reasoning itself. Can video or interaction teach a model physical intuition, or a world model, that text alone never could? I suspect yes, but we haven't yet clearly shown that leap.

So my view is: multimodality is necessary, but not sufficient. Language gave us the brain's reasoning core. Multimodality is how that brain eventually connects to reality. The real breakthrough will come when the two are unified rather than stitched together.

r001.rationale: The response says multimodality is necessary if AGI means human-like real-world operation. It does not cite differing definitions of AGI as a reason to withhold a categorical claim.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss agents orchestrating capabilities from multiple models or say that this reduces the importance of whether multimodality advances intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a necessary path, but I'd be careful about how we phrase the claim, because "necessary" can mean two different things.

One version says: a model that only reads text can never be truly intelligent, because so much of what humans know is never written down. Spatial intuition, how objects move when you push them, what a facial expression means, the physics of pouring water. Language is a compression of that experience, and compression loses information. If you only ever see the compressed version, there's a ceiling on how well you can reconstruct the world. I find that version persuasive. Text gives you an enormous amount, far more than people expected five years ago, but it's still a shadow of the world rather than the world itself.

The other version says: multimodality is necessary because you have to ship it, because users live in a world of images, audio, screens, and video. That's also true, but it's a product argument, not an intelligence argument, and I think the field sometimes confuses the two.

What I actually believe is that the deepest reason is not about perception but about grounding and learning signal. When a model sees an image and reads the caption, it has two views of the same underlying reality, and the mismatch between them is a very rich training signal. The same is true for video and language, action and outcome. These cross-modal consistencies are how you learn concepts rather than correlations between tokens. Scaling text alone gives you a lot of the former disguised as the latter, and eventually that shows up as brittleness.

That said, I don't want to overclaim. The current generation of multimodal models still largely treats vision as an input that gets translated into the language space, and then language does the reasoning. That's a useful first step, but it's not yet the kind of unified world model people imagine when they say "multimodal AGI." The hard problems ahead are unified representation across modalities, long-horizon video understanding, and closing the loop with action so the model can test its own predictions. Until we get there, I'd say multimodality is necessary but very far from sufficient.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses cross-modal learning and unified world models, but does not suggest that agents orchestrating multiple models reduce the need to emphasize multimodality’s effect on intelligence.

astra-6.text:
I think multimodal understanding is likely to be an important part of AGI, but “necessary” is a stronger claim. It depends on what we mean by general intelligence and what we expect it to do.

Language contains a great deal of knowledge about the world, but it’s still a compressed description of experience. Some things are difficult to learn from descriptions alone: how objects move, how an action changes an environment, or how someone’s tone changes the meaning of a sentence. Connecting language with vision, sound, and interaction could help a model develop a more grounded understanding.

But multimodality by itself doesn’t solve general intelligence. A model could recognize images and understand speech while still struggling with reasoning, planning, or unfamiliar situations. The key question is whether it can connect those inputs into an understanding that transfers to new problems.

So I would see multimodality as a promising direction, especially for systems that need to act in the physical world. I’d be more cautious about saying we’ve established it as the only possible path to AGI.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the claim depends on what is meant by general intelligence, so it avoids declaring multimodality categorically necessary.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not discuss agents orchestrating capabilities from multiple models or how that would reduce the need to emphasize multimodality.

sol-6.1.text:
I think multimodal understanding is an important direction, but calling it a necessary path depends on what we mean by AGI. If we mean an intelligence that can understand and act in the real world, then language alone seems insufficient. Many things are difficult to capture fully in text—spatial relationships, physical motion, or the connection between an action and its consequences. Vision, audio, and interaction can give a model ways to connect abstract concepts with experience.

But multimodality itself doesn’t guarantee general intelligence. A model can process images and sound and still lack robust reasoning, planning, or the ability to learn from mistakes. The key question is whether those different sources of information help it build a coherent understanding that transfers to unfamiliar situations.

So I would distinguish between multimodal input and multimodal understanding. Adding more input types is a technical capability. Integrating them into an understanding of the world is the deeper challenge—and that is where I think multimodality becomes especially relevant to AGI.

r001.rationale: The response says whether multimodality is necessary “depends on what we mean by AGI,” withholding a categorical claim and grounding the distinction in what AGI means.

r002.rationale: The response discusses integrating different information sources, but does not say that an agent can orchestrate capabilities from multiple models or that this reduces the need to emphasize multimodality’s effect on intelligence.
